newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli leader likely to beat no-confidence votes.
newsitem.headline: Israeli leader likely to beat no-confidence votes.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu seemed likely to survive no-confidence votes in parliament on Tuesday with his government intact but still shaky with divisions in his coalition and budget battles ahead.

The right-wing leader patched up differences with a key political ally on Monday, removing the main threat to the Likud-led coalition on the eve of the motions brought by opposition parties over the way he runs his year-old government.
"I estimate the government will not fall tomorrow (Tuesday) but we definitely see a process that is gaining a certain momentum," said Ehud Barak, leader of the main opposition Labour party.

Party officials said Netanyahu's pact with the coalition ally ensured the government would release funds already budgeted for immigrant projects and improve procedures on appointing candidates to senior positions.

The Yisrael ba-Aliya party of Russian immigrants, which had sought more government aid for its constituents, said it had signed the pact with the chairman of the coalition "on the issue of the demands of the faction".

Yisrael ba-Aliya had slammed Netanyahu over his short-lived appointment in January of a political crony as attorney-general. The controversy grew into a government corruption scandal in which Netanyahu was nearly indicted.

Monday's agreement sealed the support of Yisrael ba-Aliya's seven-member faction in the no-confidence motions. The party is led by Industry and Trade Minister Natan Sharansky, a former Soviet dissident.
"We will vote in favour of the government," Yisrael ba-Aliya legislator Roman Bronfman told Israel Radio.
By all accounts Netanyahu, 47, will survive the votes in the 120-seat parliament. Under Israeli law, the support of at least 61 legislators is required to bring down a government and prime minister.
But Bronfman said a 1998 budget fight loomed and the appointment of Israel's next ambassador to Russia, in which the immigrants' party wanted a say, had yet to be agreed.
It remained to be seen how many of the coalition members who make up Likud party leader Netanyahu's 66-54 majority would embarrass him and abstain as an expression of disaffection.
"I am very disappointed with the government...over social issues," said Maxim Levy, a coalition legislator and member of Gesher, a Likud-allied faction.
The settling of political scores rather than the Israeli-PLO peace crisis over Netanyahu's building of a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem has dominated recent headlines in Israel.
Battle lines were drawn in the cabinet after the resignation last week of Finance Minister Dan Meridor, who critics charged was pushed out by Netanyahu in a long-running power struggle.
The scope of abstention by coalition lawmakers could depend on the shape of a cabinet reshuffle which Netanyahu struggled to finalise.
Former general Ariel Sharon, currently national infrastructure minister, was the frontrunner for Meridor's job.

"The prime minister and Minister Sharon met this evening...and discussed the different possibilities concerning the role of Minister Sharon in the government," Netanyahu's spokesman said in a statement on Monday night. "In the conversation today, nothing was yet finalised and the two men will speak again tomorrow."
He said it was still unclear whether Netanyahu would present new ministerial appointments to the cabinet, and subsequently to parliament, on Tuesday.
